Derivative budgets and unique jets

Written by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

A smooth function can have every derivative zero at one point and still be nonzero elsewhere. A sufficiently restrictive derivative budget prevents this. The decisive numerical test uses the lower convex boundary of the logarithms of that budget. Large allowances at isolated orders may have no effect: bounds at the intervening orders can already force uniqueness.

We prove the criterion for every positive sequence, without assuming monotonicity or logarithmic convexity. Its converse constructs compact smooth functions with the prescribed bounds. For the derivative-growth scales used in wavefront analysis, the criterion determines exactly when compact cutoffs exist. These cutoffs give one compact Fourier witness valid at every order.

The fundamental theorem, uniform limits and compact extrema have the proofs in the scalar foundation, Sections 12–13, especially 13.4, 13.5 and 13.7. The integral Taylor formula is proved in When a kernel is smooth. Product integration, domination and affine substitution are proved in the integration foundation, Sections 15–16. Summable smoothing and fixed Fourier tests, Lemma 1 and Theorems 4 and 6, supplies the full infinite-convolution construction, the compact-cutoff equivalence and the fixed Fourier-witness theorem. The scales and their localization estimates are those of Derivative growth and finite-order localization and Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts.

The numerical test for derivative-growth wavefronts

Corollary 5. Let , . For the class with local bounds , the following alternatives hold.

  • If , a zero infinite jet at one point of a connected open set forces the function to be zero everywhere on that set. There is no nonzero compact function in this class on .

Proof. In one dimension set , with . The constants and define the same class: enlarge to dominate ; conversely take . Since is nondecreasing, the sequence called in (J2) is precisely this given sequence. Theorem 4 gives its exact criterion.

In several dimensions restrict a function to a line segment in a compact ball inside its domain. The repeated directional derivative has the multinomial expansion The expansion follows by induction using commuting smooth partial derivatives, and its absolute coefficient sum is the finite multinomial formula. A flat jet therefore makes the restriction zero along every segment from that point in the ball. Thus the zero-jet set is open; it is closed relative to the domain by continuity of every derivative. Connectedness makes a nonempty such set the whole domain. A compact function has an open zero set outside a ball, proving the first alternative.

In the convergent case (J14) gives a nonquasianalytic one-dimensional witness. The full compact-cutoff equivalence in Theorem 4 of the summable-smoothing lesson gives the cutoffs in every dimension, with all algebra estimates proved there. Its Theorem 6 then gives (J15) and its converse with the same bounded-distribution and cone quantifiers. Its denominator can be replaced by : on double the exponential constant, while on use the bounded Fourier transform on that compact set and , enlarging to at least two. The reverse replacement only weakens the bound. The numerical hypothesis needed for the earlier theorem is supplied by Theorem 4 here.
